name: Society Turn PUD
keyQuestion: Should a 400,000 sq ft medical campus and hotel at Society Turn — the largest development ever proposed in San Miguel County — be evaluated for its cumulative regional impact before approval?
whyItMatters: At 400,000 sq ft, the Society Turn PUD would be the largest single development in county history. Combined with the nearby Four Seasons, it would bring an estimated 1,058 new employees to an already capacity-constrained region — with no identified housing plan for those workers.

name: SMART Gondola & Measure 3A
jurisdiction: SMART (San Miguel Authority for Regional Transportation)
keyQuestion: Is the gondola capital program appropriately scoped and financed, and what is the true cost of long-term operations and debt service to regional taxpayers?
whyItMatters: SMART's gondola program carries an estimated $40M in public debt. Measure 3A was a ballot issue asking voters to authorize additional bonding. The gondola is the primary public transit link between Telluride and Mountain Village — its financing and governance affect every resident and visitor in the region.
costNote: Confirmed — $40M public bond authorization (Measure 3A); full project cost not publicly disclosed.

name: VooDoo Affordable Housing
keyQuestion: With a $23M balloon payment due around 2032, how does the Town plan to refinance or repay the VooDoo project debt — and what happens if market conditions don't cooperate?
whyItMatters: VooDoo is a 27-unit affordable housing project financed with approximately $27.4 million in public funds. A balloon payment of roughly $23 million comes due around 2032. The project demonstrates both the community's commitment to workforce housing and the fiscal risks of the financing model used.
costNote: Confirmed — $27.4M public financing per Town debt records. 27 units / $1,015,000 per unit.

name: Chair 7 / Former Hotel Development
jurisdiction: San Miguel County Open Space District
keyQuestion: Was the Chair 7 area effectively dedicated to the Open Space District in 1979, and does a former hotel concept on that land honor or violate that public commitment?
whyItMatters: In 1979, the Chair 7 area was understood by many to be dedicated to San Miguel County's Open Space District. A subsequent hotel development concept raised questions about whether that public land commitment can be unwound decades later.

name: Four Seasons Resort and Residences Telluride
keyQuestion: The Four Seasons is housing hundreds of construction workers in Naturita, Ridgway, and the West End — communities that say they 'already operate at full capacity.' Who pays when the burdens fall down-valley but the benefits flow inward to Mountain Village?
whyItMatters: The $1 billion Four Seasons broke ground October 2025 and is under active construction — 36 months, finishing ~2028. It has 52 hotel rooms, 43 hotel residences, 26 private residences (priced $4M–$35M at $5,500/sq ft), and only 10 employee apartments for an operation that will require hundreds of permanent staff. Construction is already forcing workers into Naturita (42-room Rimrock Hotel, purchased by developer), Camp V, and Ridgway — where the Town of Ridgway filed a lawsuit in March 2026 against the MTN Lodge for housing workers in a commercially-zoned hotel. Norwood Mayor Candy Meehan called it 'saturation at an unprecedented level.' A coalition of West End leaders sent a letter in July 2025 demanding a 'community benefit agreement,' saying the resort's benefits 'flow inward' while the burdens fall on communities 'who anticipate few, if any, long-term benefits.' The developer made a $2.5M contribution toward Telluride affordable housing — a fraction of the $580M in financing.
costNote: Confirmed — $1B announced project cost per developer/media; $417.5M construction loan. 52 hotel rooms / $19,231,000 per room.

name: Six Senses Telluride
keyQuestion: Six Senses houses 56 employees on-site — the most workforce housing per square foot of any hotel in North America, developers claim. But a 77-room luxury resort will employ far more than 56 people. Where do the rest live, and what does that mean for a region already at capacity?
whyItMatters: Six Senses Telluride is a $285 million, 77-room luxury resort being developed on the last large hotel site in Mountain Village, approved by Mountain Village Town Council and targeting a 2028 opening. It is the first Six Senses property in the U.S. and IHG's first luxury mountain resort in North America's Mountain West. The project dedicates 14,000–15,000 sq ft to employee housing for 56 staff — which developers describe as the most workforce housing per square foot of any hotel in North America. But a 77-room full-service luxury resort with rooftop pool, Omakase dining, speakeasy bar, spa, and 24 residences will require substantially more than 56 operational employees. Viewed alongside the Four Seasons (52 rooms, opening same year), this is 129 new luxury hotel rooms added to Mountain Village in one construction cycle — all drawing from the same regional workforce with no regional housing plan to match.
costNote: Confirmed — $285M announced project cost per developer/media. 77 hotel rooms / $3,701,000 per room.

name: Aldasoro PUD / Diamond Ranch
keyQuestion: Is the county enforcing the conditions of the Aldasoro PUD, and what does the Diamond Ranch litigation reveal about how San Miguel County oversees approved PUD conditions long-term?
whyItMatters: Case 2023CV30044 involves enforcement of the Aldasoro PUD in Diamond Ranch. The case raises broader questions about how San Miguel County oversees approved planned unit developments over time — and what happens when conditions aren't enforced.

name: Shandoka / Lot L Housing Projects
keyQuestion: What are the total public costs associated with Shandoka and Lot L, and how does each project's financing model compare to alternatives?
whyItMatters: Shandoka and Lot L represent the Town of Telluride's major in-town affordable housing development sites. Decisions about density, financing, and ownership structure at these locations will shape the Town's housing stock for decades.

name: Sunnyside Housing Project
keyQuestion: How does the Sunnyside project address Telluride's documented workforce housing shortage, and at what public cost per unit?
whyItMatters: The Sunnyside project is one of several housing initiatives aimed at addressing Telluride's severe shortage of workforce housing. The project's financing structure and unit count will affect how many workers can afford to live in town rather than commuting 25+ miles daily.

name: Hospital District / Medical Facility — Society Turn Context
keyQuestion: How does the proposed hospital district footprint at Society Turn interact with the broader PUD review, and is co-location with a 125-room hotel and 400,000 sq ft commercial campus appropriate?
whyItMatters: A medical facility proposed in the Society Turn area is part of the broader context for the Society Turn PUD review. The combination of medical, hotel, and commercial uses at this corridor raises questions about cumulative impacts and community priorities for scarce highway-adjacent land.

name: Carhenge Lot Redevelopment
location: SW Telluride — surface parking lot near Lift 7

upcomingHearings.description: Consideration of an application for a Work Session on proposed new construction on Town property, pursuant to LUC 5-201.C

keyQuestion: The Town of Telluride is proposing to redevelop the Carhenge parking lot — Town-owned land at the base of Lift 7 — into a mixed-use housing and commercial neighborhood. What is the cost, who benefits, and what say does the public have before it's built?
whyItMatters: The Carhenge site (Lots 34 and 34B) is a Town-owned surface parking lot in southwest Telluride. The Town and Design Workshop are advancing a concept for mixed-use housing, underground parking, and community-serving commercial uses through a full entitlement gauntlet: HARC design review, PUD, Subdivision, and Large Scale Activity applications. As of May 2026 the project is in HARC work session review, with a broader public hearing process ahead. This is one of the last large, Town-owned development sites in Telluride proper.
costNote: Estimate — based on Canyonlands/Tower House comparable ($867/SF all-in ex-land) applied to 213,400 SF above-grade program (sum of Buildings A–F per Exhibit C site plan), plus 230 underground parking spaces × $60,000/space. Town-owned land ($0 acquisition). 230 units / $864,000 per unit.

name: Norwood / Wright's Mesa Housing & Infrastructure
jurisdiction: Town of Norwood / San Miguel County
keyQuestion: Are housing and infrastructure investments in Norwood and Wright's Mesa keeping pace with population pressures from Telluride-area workers priced out of the east end?
whyItMatters: Norwood and Wright's Mesa serve as the agricultural and working-class heart of San Miguel County. Workers priced out of Telluride increasingly commute from this area — 25+ miles each way. Housing and infrastructure decisions here shape whether down-valley communities remain economically viable.

name: Nucla / Naturita / West End Economic Development
jurisdiction: San Miguel County / Town of Nucla / Town of Naturita
keyQuestion: As the West End transitions away from coal and uranium extraction, what public investments and civic infrastructure are being planned to support economic diversification and long-term community stability?
whyItMatters: The Nucla-Naturita corridor represents the West End of San Miguel County — a community in economic transition after the decline of extraction industries. Major civic and infrastructure decisions in this area will determine whether these communities stabilize or decline, affecting the county's fiscal balance and regional identity.

name: Canyonlands / Tower House Affordable Housing
location: West Telluride — near Clark's Market, Colorado Ave corridor

documents.title: Canyonlands / Tower House Community Presentation — June 2023

keyQuestion: The Town of Telluride acquired two parcels near Clark's Market (Tower House in 2018, Canyonlands in 2021) specifically for affordable housing. What will be built, at what cost, and who will it serve?
whyItMatters: These two Town-owned parcels — 0.33 AC Tower House and 0.20 AC Canyonlands — represent some of the last infill land in west Telluride purchased specifically for affordable housing. The 2023 program called for 35–45 units, ~85% deed-restricted at 80–150% AMI, with a mix of rental and for-sale units. Construction is now underway (basement level as of May 2026). The San Miguel County Housing Needs Assessment estimated a shortfall of 800+ units by 2026 — this project is one of the Town's direct responses.
costNote: Estimate — $3M land + $26M construction loan + $4.7M soft costs (18%) + $1.4M water/sewer tap fee waivers (~35 taps × $40K). 40 units / $877,000 per unit.
